y-m-81-05.prereq.0: H3 only batch difficulty/support label, no grade assignment. Math and Culture assumes high-school math basics (numbers, expressions, functions, simple probability).
y-m-81-05.title: How many Hangul syllables have no final consonant?
y-m-81-05.goal: Distinguish ratio of possible forms from actual writing frequency; state info/method needed for latter.
y-m-81-05.material: Modern Hangul syllable has initial consonant, vowel, and optional final batchim. For task count 19 initials,21 vowels,28 finals incl none. Assume any can combine; count possible forms, not actual usage.
y-m-81-05.thinking.1: Distinguish possible cases from real use frequency
y-m-81-05.prereq.2: Can read Hangul letter names (material explains initial/vowel/final).
y-m-81-05.s.s1.prompt: Estimate: roughly what fraction of possible syllables have no final?
y-m-81-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write counts with and without final using initial/vowel/final counts.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.hint.1: When ratio of counts, what happen to initial and vowel numbers?
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.a: You compare no-final cases to all cases; initial/vowel counts cancel.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.b: No final is 1 of 28 final options. Recalculate fraction 1/28. [1 28 28]
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.c: Calling no-final share one-eighth of 28 too large; initial and vowel multiply both groups equally.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.d: You split into has final/no final and think half. Final case has 27 options.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.explain: No-final forms=19×21=399; total=19×21×28=11172. Ratio 399/11172=1/28≈3.6%. Initial/vowel factors cancel, leaving 1 of 28 finals.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.prompt: Student sees ratio and says real writing also has no-final letters only at this rate. What think?
y-m-81-05.s.s2.hint.0: Are possible form count and how often used the same?
y-m-81-05.s.s2.hint.1: If each syllable used same number of times, what follows? Is that assumption true?
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.a: No. But longer text automatically approaches 3.6%.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.a: Long-text settled rate is writing frequency, not possible-form ratio.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.b: Cannot tell. Maybe 28 final types wrong.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.b: 28 is task convention. Issue is whether count ratio becomes usage frequency.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.c: No. Need know each letter usage frequency.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.c: You distinguish possible forms from actual uses; actual frequency needs separate investigation.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.d: Yes. Ratio of possible letters same as writing ratio.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.d: Possible-form ratio differs from usage ratio; depend how often each is used.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.explain: 11172 is possible forms. Real writing uses some syllables often, others rarely. Without equal-frequency assumption, count ratio cannot become use ratio.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.prompt: How find no-final syllable frequency in real writing? Give method and one limitation.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.hint.0: Choose text and count syllables in two groups (no final/has final).
y-m-81-05.s.s3.hint.1: Would one text result be reliable?
y-m-81-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state text choice, counting process, and ratio calculation?
y-m-81-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: For limitation, did you specify what method cannot tell?
y-m-81-05.s.s3.model.0: Choose text, count no-final syllables/total. One text may be unusual, so use several and count same way.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.model.1: Choose one book page, count no-final and all syllables, find ratio. Writing type affects result, so compare poems, explanations, etc.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: You say limitation is dependence on text type.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.model.2: Count no-final letters in one text and find ratio; one text may be biased by its style.

y-m-81-02.title: Let's design leap-year rule ourselves
y-m-81-02.goal: Understand leap rule sets average year length; design multiple rules meeting conditions, compare/explain errors.
y-m-81-02.material: Earth's orbit year (tropical year) ~365.2422 days. Calendar year 365 or 366 days; choose every how many years to add day. Write rule 'L leap days in N-year cycle'; average=365+L/N. Assume tropical year 365.2422 and compare average drift from seasons.
y-m-81-02.thinking.2: Find error in a rule description
y-m-81-02.prereq.0: H3 only batch difficulty/support label, no grade assignment. Math and Culture assumes high-school math basics (numbers, expressions, functions, simple probability).
y-m-81-02.s.s1.prompt: Estimate first: if add leap day once every 4 years and continue, how far calendar drift from seasons after 1000 years? [4 4 1000]
y-m-81-02.s.s1.hint.0: For 4-year rule, write average year length beside 365.2422 and compare.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think how yearly small difference accumulates 1000 times.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.a: Maybe yearly difference too small or place value lost when multiplying years.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.b: You estimate yearly difference ~10 times too big. Recalculate difference between 4-year average and 365.2422.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.o.c: About 8 days (a bit over a week)
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.c: You multiply small yearly difference by number of years.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.o.d: No drift because leap years exist.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.d: Even with leap years, unequal average causes accumulated drift. Compare averages.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.explain: 4-year rule average is 365.25, tropical year ~365.2422: gap 0.0078 day yearly. Over 1000 years about 7.8 days, ~8 days.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.prompt: Now design. Rule L leap days per N years: make 2 different rules with average (365+L/N) within 0.0005 day of 365.2422. N natural ≤400, L integer ≥0.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.hint.0: For average 365+L/N, ratio L/N must be near 0.2422. Choose N then adjust L, compare ratio.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.hint.1: Try whether smaller or larger N makes it easier to get error in range.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Average differs from 365.2422 by more than 0.0005 day.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.explain: Examples: 8 days/33 years (avg ~365.2424), 31/128 (365.2421875), 97/400 (365.2425), all fit. Same ratio L/N counts as same rule (e.g. 8/33 and 16/66). Many others fit.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain with at least one number why your rule drifts less than leap day every 4 years.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare your average and 4-year average 365.25 each with 365.2422.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put yearly accumulated differences side by side.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You compare both rules on same basis (yearly average or same centuries)? [4]
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You show evidence with at least two numbers, not just 'more accurate'?
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.model.0: My rule 97 in 400 years gives avg 365.2425, gap 0.0003 from 365.2422. 4-year rule avg 365.25, gap 0.0078 yearly, so my rule drifts much less.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.model.1: With 8 days in 33 years, yearly avg ~365.2424, error ~0.0002 days, much smaller than 0.0078 for 4-year rule; even after 1000 years drift under a day.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: I add numeric estimate under one day after 1000 years too.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.prompt: This text explains leap-year rule used in many countries. Which line is wrong?
y-m-81-02.s.s3.hint.0: For each line pick example year and apply earlier rules.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.hint.1: Plug conclusion-line years into rules one by one.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.1: But divisible by 100 is not leap.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.3: Therefore 1900, 2000, 2100 all divisible by 100, so common years.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.4: This rule average slightly under 365.25, thus closer to 365.2422 than every-four-year rule. [365.25 365.2422 4]
y-m-81-02.s.s3.explain: Line 4 wrong: 2000 divisible by 100 and 400, so line 3 makes it leap. 1900 and 2100 common. Line 5 right: 400 years has 100 multiples of 4, remove 4 multiples of 100, add 1 multiple of 400 =97 leap days; avg 365.2425, closer to 365.2422 than 365.25. [4 2000 100 400 3 1900 2100 5 400 4 100 100 4 1 400 97 365.2425 365.2422 4 365.25]

y-m-81-03.prereq.0: H3 only batch difficulty/support label, no grade assignment. Math and Culture assumes high-school math basics (numbers, expressions, functions, simple probability).
y-m-81-03.title: Throwing yut sticks: is every result equally likely?
y-m-81-03.goal: Separate outcomes from equal-likelihood; update yut/mo comparison when data/conditions change; state info needed.
y-m-81-03.material: Yut game: toss 4 sticks together; result based on count flat belly side up. 1 belly=do, 2=gae, 3=geol, 4=yut, 0 (all rounded backs)=mo. Assume sticks independent; chance one lands belly-up p. Real p depends on stick construction.
y-m-81-03.thinking.0: Find first line where error begins
y-m-81-03.prereq.1: Count cases (product rule), multiply independent probabilities, percent and ratios
y-m-81-03.prereq.2: Even if never played yut, use only rules in text.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.prompt: Student explain yut-stick probabilities below. Assume one stick belly-up chance p=1/2. Which line first wrong?
y-m-81-03.s.s1.hint.0: Label sticks ①②③④ and list how many of 16 patterns have exactly one belly. [16 1]
y-m-81-03.s.s1.hint.1: Table count how many of 16 patterns give do, gae, geol, yut, mo; compare.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.0: There are five result types: do, gae, geol, yut, mo.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.1: Four sticks each belly/back gives 2×2×2×2=16 patterns; if p=1/2 all 16 equally likely. [4 2 2 2 2 16 1 2 16]
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.2: But there are five outcomes, so each equally likely.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.3: So probability yut na 1/5, and probability mo too na 1/5.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.explain: First mistake line 3. Five outcomes no mean equally likely. Of 16 patterns: do (1 belly) get 4, gae 6, geol 4, yut and mo 1 each. Probabilities 4/16,6/16,4/16,1/16,1/16. Line 4 follows wrong line 3. [3 5 16 1 4 6 4 1 4 16 6 16 4 16 1 16 1 16 4 3]
y-m-81-03.s.s2.prompt: Info arrive one by one. Each time judge: “Which happen more, yut (4 bellies) or mo (4 backs)?”
y-m-81-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think how strongly current info determine p.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write yut and mo probability as product of each stick belly/back probability.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.info: All 4 ideal sticks have p=1/2. Among 16 patterns, yut all belly=1 and mo all backs=1.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.ask: Which happen more, yut or mo?
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.ask: Which happen more, yut or mo?
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.after: If p=1/2 both 1/16, equal. Real stick p may not exactly half. [1 2 1 16 1 2]
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.o.a: Yut more; belly more naturally face upward.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.r.a: You assume p=1/2, so belly/back equally likely. This reason no fit assumption given.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.o.b: Mo more; mo move far, so must be harder.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.r.b: High score and low probability different. Under this assumption compare pattern counts.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.o.c: Both one pattern out of 16, so equally often. [1 16]
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.r.c: You count patterns; comparison relies on p=1/2 assumption.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.info: You toss one real yut stick 100 times; belly up 60 times (all four sticks same shape).
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.ask: After this data, wetin think about yut and mo?
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.after: Chance of ≥60 out of 100 if p=1/2 about 3%. Uncommon but possible; either think p>0.5 or keep first judgment if state evidence. If p=0.6, yut≈0.130 and mo≈0.026, about 5 times likely.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.a: It was 60, so p fixed at 0.6 and yut about 5 times more often.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.a: 100 tosses not many. 0.6 estimate, not fixed; could be 0.55 or 0.65.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.b: p may be around 0.6, so yut may happen more, but be careful how much more.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.b: You mention estimate uncertainty; judgment ties data amount to confidence.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.c: Belly came 60, back 40, so yut:mo also 60:40, about 1.5 times.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.c: Yut needs all four bellies, so multiply p four times. No use single-stick ratio directly.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.d: 60 of 100 can happen by chance, so little reason still to abandon p=1/2.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.d: You consider chance range and keep first view; could also see when result too far to explain by chance.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.info: Four sticks differ: two belly probability 0.6, two 0.4; independent.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.after: Yut=0.6×0.6×0.4×0.4=0.0576; mo=0.4×0.4×0.6×0.6=0.0576, equal. If all p same, equal only p=1/2; different p values can also equal like this.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.o.a: Yut more often because some sticks p=0.6.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.a: Some p=.6 but some .4. Write yut/mo probability products and compare. [0.6 0.4]
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.b: Independence lets multiply probabilities. Check if needed probabilities provided.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.o.c: Mo more because some sticks have low belly probability.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.c: Mo also needs 0.6 stick land back, probability 0.4.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.d: You write each as product and see same values, belly/back swapped.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.reflect: How did p=1/2 judgment change after 100 tosses and after learning stick probabilities differ? Did info change view or confidence?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.prompt: What extra info needed to say yut and mo equally likely, and how compare then?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side how each stick must land for yut and mo.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.hint.1: Which values needed to compare numerically?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is info you wrote actually used to calculate both probabilities?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish all p same vs each stick differs?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.model.0: Need each stick belly-up probability. If all four same p, yut/mo equal only p=1/2; if different, compare product belly probs with product back probs.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.model.1: Need each stick belly probability and whether independent. Multiply belly probabilities for yut and back probs for mo, then compare.

y-m-81-06.prereq.0: H3 only batch difficulty/support label, no grade assignment. Math and Culture assumes high-school math basics (numbers, expressions, functions, simple probability).
y-m-81-06.title: If one vertex works, does whole tiling work?
y-m-81-06.topic: Regular polygon patterns and tessellating plane
y-m-81-06.goal: Find angle combinations summing 360° at one vertex; judge why this alone cannot prove plane coverage.
y-m-81-06.material: Tiles regular polygons with no gaps/overlaps. Angles meeting at a vertex sum 360°. Regular n-gon angle set by n; triangle 60°, square 90°, hexagon 120°. Only 3 polygons meet per vertex; 3≤n≤50. [360 60 90 120 3 50]
y-m-81-06.prereq.1: Regular polygon interior angles; solve fractions/equations
y-m-81-06.s.s1.prompt: Guess: besides (6,6,6), what triples of regular polygons at one vertex sum 360? n≤50.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.hint.0: If one triangle angle 60°, find required sum of other two.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.hint.1: Use same method with one square (90°), find several combinations.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.a: Other polygons such as octagon have angles too. Try one or two.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.b: Check combinations without triangle too, including pentagon or octagon.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.c: You leave open other polygons; count combinations directly.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.d: Hard to justify only one more. Count combinations with polygons besides triangle, square, hexagon.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.explain: Next step count finds 10 total including (6,6,6).
y-m-81-06.s.s2.prompt: Find 4 different triples regular a,b,c-gons meeting at vertex, angles sum exactly 360°. 3≤a≤b≤c≤50 integers; order permutations same.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.hint.0: Table regular n-gon angle sizes, starting n=3.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.hint.1: Choose smallest a, find required sum of other two angles, then vary b.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.prompt: Among (5,5,10), two pentagons and decagon fit 360° at one vertex. Can this alone make gap-free plane pattern?
y-m-81-06.s.s3.hint.0: Draw neighboring vertices around one decagon side; check same combo continues.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.hint.1: If two pentagons share side, check neighboring vertex also fits combo.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.a: One vertex match not enough; check neighbors separately.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.a: You distinguish one-point fit from fit everywhere; necessary vs sufficient.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.b: Only (4,6,12), all three kinds, can tile plane gap-free.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.b: (6,6,6) and (4,8,8) also tile. Number of polygon types not criterion.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.c: Angles fit one vertex, so repeating will always tile.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.c: 360° at one vertex necessary; neighboring vertices also need work. []
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.d: Number of vertex combos always equals number of tilings.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.d: Question is whether every combo tiles. No reason counts equal.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.explain: 360° is necessary, not sufficient. Of ten above, known tilings include (3,12,12),(4,6,12),(4,8,8),(6,6,6); (5,5,10) fails as continuing to neighboring vertices conflicts. [360 10 3 12 12 4 6 12 4 8 8 6 6 6 5 5 10]
